Confidence intervals for dependability and SEM in D-study plans

Source: R/api-multivariate-dstudy-intervals.R
confint.mfrm_multivariate_d_study.Rd

Quantify uncertainty in relative G, absolute dependability Phi or measurement SEM for specified future counts of common tasks, raters or other random facets. Most methods use a complete balanced ANOVA source. An explicitly selected experimental REML profile also accepts identifiable incomplete MINQUE sources for G/Phi and SEM; future plans still describe complete balanced ratings. For one-facet relative SEM, residual contrasts also accept incomplete sources without likelihood fitting, under the normal residual model. For one-facet G, explicit spectral F intervals accept incomplete sources under independent normal Person effects and residuals. Explicit delta-method coefficient SEs and normal-reference intervals also use the original ANOVA/MINQUE estimator for supported crossed/nested sources.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'mfrm_multivariate_d_study'
confint(
  object,
  parm = "G",
  level = 0.95,
  score = NULL,
  composite = NULL,
  assumption,
  draws = 100000L,
  seed = 1L,
  reference = NULL,
  method = "auto",
  ...
)

Arguments

object

A result from mfrm_d_study() based on a balanced ANOVA G-study with one or two crossed random measurement facets, or the supported balanced nested design. Nested G/Phi defaults require unchanged source child counts per parent; changed counts require an explicit experimental method. See "Nested plans" below. For G/Phi and SEM, method = "reml_profile" also accepts an incomplete or unequal MINQUE source with its original used ratings retained in the object. method = "residual_contrast" accepts retained one-facet ANOVA/MINQUE ratings for parm = "RelativeSEM" only, including plan differences. method = "spectral_f" accepts these sources for parm = "G", including plan differences, with positive residual degrees of freedom. method = "delta" accepts ANOVA or identifiable MINQUE sources for individual-plan G/Phi, including changed nested child counts. MINQUE requires retained assignments and moment inputs for its sampling covariance.

parm

One of "G" (default), "Phi", "RelativeSEM" or "AbsoluteSEM". With reference, return differences in that metric for the selected source and supported method.

level

Confidence level strictly between zero and one.

score

One original score name.

composite

One named composite, or "Composite" for vector weights. Select either score or composite. With neither specified, select the sole composite, or the first original score if no composite is present. Multiple composites require a selection. Weights must be prespecified.

assumption

Required: "normal" asserts independent normal random effects with constant component variances. The source persons and facet levels are sampled from their intended populations. This is not tested.

draws

Number of independent pivotal draws for one-facet Phi GCI, default 100000. Must be an integer at least 1000, with at least 100 expected draws in each tail at the requested level. Increase it when the returned endpoint Monte Carlo bands are too wide for the intended decision. Unused by other methods.

seed

Nonnegative integer seed for one-facet Phi GCI, default 1. The caller's random seed is preserved. The current R RNG kind is used and recorded. Unused by other methods.

reference

Optional row number in object$design_grid. Return each other plan's selected metric minus this reference plan's value. The default supports one-facet sources and nested plans with a common future child count (unchanged from the source for G/Phi). Map the whole F set for G or generalized interval for Phi, preserving their different coverage qualifications. Explicit method = "reml_profile" also supports crossed/nested plans changing both facet counts, including incomplete/unequal sources. One-facet and common-child nested plans map a shared profile interval; other comparisons constrain the difference directly, using optional nloptr. Its calibration remains experimental, especially at zero differences. For general two-facet crossed/nested comparisons, explicitly select method = "mean_square_region" for a conservative joint-region enclosure for G, Phi or SEM. Approximate-F differences are not supplied. At least two plans are required. NULL returns individual-plan intervals.

method

"auto" (default) selects "exact_f" for one-facet G and "gci" for one-facet Phi, including the nested reduction below. For individual G/Phi with two crossed random facets, it selects "mls", an approximate signed-MLS null inversion with conservative completion of undefined widths; see "Two-crossed-facet MLS intervals" below. To compare other choices, or for nested plans with changed child counts, select "approximate_f", "mean_square_region", or a vector containing both to compare methods on the same data and target. Neither is an automatic default. "mls" can also be compared with these methods for crossed G/Phi. "mean_square_region" requires the optional lpSolve package. Balanced two-crossed-facet G also accepts explicit "score", an approximate score inversion with extended nuisance parameters. It uses stored mean squares, preserves original points and requires no optional optimizer package. It can be compared with the other supported G methods. It is not a Phi, SEM, nested, incomplete-source or reference method. For SEM, "auto" selects "mls": a single contributing mean square uses its chi-square interval; positive sums use Graybill-Wang MLS and signed sums use Ting MLS. This is a specified calculation rule, not selection based on which interval looks favorable. Method records the calculation used for each plan. Two-facet crossed/nested SEM also accepts "mean_square_region", using linear error-variance projections followed by square roots. Select one method at a time unless including "reml_profile", or comparing supported experimental coefficient methods above. "reml_profile" is an explicit G/Phi or SEM choice for balanced or incomplete sources. It requires optional lme4 and minqa, fits a separate normal REML model, and retains the original point estimate. It can be compared with other methods for the same supported target in a vector; reference uses a shared interval image or a direct difference profile as described below. The latter additionally requires nloptr. Its chi-square calibration is approximate, especially at component boundaries. It is never selected automatically. No fallback follows a failed calculation. Explicit "residual_contrast" supplies one-facet RelativeSEM intervals and differences from retained ANOVA/MINQUE ratings without likelihood fitting or simulation. It maps one residual chi-square interval, preserves original points and reports the separate projected IntervalCenter. It can be compared with MLS or REML for this supported target. It is not an AbsoluteSEM, G/Phi or multifacet method; see Residual-contrast SEM. Explicit "spectral_f" supplies one-facet G intervals and paired differences from retained ANOVA/MINQUE ratings. It removes facet effects and inverts an exact normal-model F pivot without likelihood fitting or simulation. It preserves original points and can be compared with "exact_f" (balanced sources) or "reml_profile". It is not an automatically selected, Phi, SEM, nested or multifacet method. Explicit "delta" supplies G/Phi sampling SEs and normal-reference intervals from the original component estimator and its full sampling covariance. It accepts supported one-facet, crossed and nested sources, including incomplete MINQUE, and can be included in a method vector. It requires no refitting or simulation. It is not a SEM or reference method. Defaults are unchanged; see Delta coefficient SEs and intervals.

...

Reserved; additional arguments are rejected.

Value

A data frame of class mfrm_dstudy_intervals, with scenario/facet counts, Kind, Score, Metric, Estimate, PointStatus, Lower, Upper, unrestricted RawRatioLower and RawRatioUpper (balanced F/GCI coefficient methods), Level, Method, interval Status, MethodCode, Available, NegativeComponent, and Validation. Each selected method supplies a row per plan, including unavailable rows. Delta results additionally supply SE, SamplingVariance, SEStatus, AtBoundary, OutsideParameterSpace and SamplingCovariancePSD. Attribute sampling_covariance retains the component covariance with its own diagnostics and weights divided by their largest absolute value; weights retains the original score definition. Row-aligned diagnostics records normalized gradients, error coefficients and scales. MINQUE results retain source_data for source-identity checks. Method comparisons including delta retain the complete per-method objects in method_results. Spectral F additionally supplies LogVarianceRatioLower/Upper and projection/root diagnostics in pivot; it does not supply a replacement point estimate or SE. Coefficient MLS additionally retains NumericalComplete, FormulaComplete and Empty. Its row-aligned diagnostics contain the null problem, quadratic coefficients, accepted pieces/nodes, and any conservatively retained undefined ranges. Formula completeness and numerical availability are separate from the approximate statistical calibration. Score intervals additionally retain NumericalComplete and Empty to distinguish a resolved empty numerical set from a failed calculation; either has missing accepted endpoints. Scanned pieces and root checks remain in the row-aligned diagnostics attribute. plot() compares saved intervals without recomputation. design_grid retains future counts. For two facets, diagnostics is a row-aligned list of F moments/roots or solver status/residuals; mean_squares stores the normalized source mean squares, their scale, df and component map. Attributes weights, assumption, source_design, source_rows, pivot (G's log ratio/endpoints and degrees of freedom; Phi's single-rating bounds and degrees of freedom), and notes retain context. For Phi, RawRatioLower/Upper are NA because there is no G-type F ratio; monte_carlo retains numerical precision diagnostics. Phi endpoints and their numerical bands are withheld when a positive width rounds away. If the base pivotal interval has lost resolution, plan differences also remain unavailable, including identical-count comparisons. The pivot attribute retains the diagnostic base bounds. A sampled atom at zero retains its separate "Upper endpoint at zero" status. Save the whole object with saveRDS(). source_summary retains the design, covariance components, mean products and degrees of freedom for checking that a curve overlay uses the same source. REML profiles additionally retain source_data to check the used ratings, reml_source with the fit and numerical diagnostics, and row-aligned profile diagnostics with scans, accepted pieces, optimizer attempts and gradient checks. No live fitting environment is saved. IntervalCenter is the separate REML estimate; CandidateLower/Upper can remain finite when accepted bounds are unavailable. Shared-image REML reference results retain the common fit and scans in base_interval, with row-aligned transformation data in diagnostics. Direct difference profiles instead retain per-comparison scans and constraints in diagnostics, and all reference counts in attr(result, "reference")$counts. Residual-contrast SEM also retains source_data and a separate IntervalCenter; base_interval contains the residual variance interval, residual_projection its numerical checks, and row-aligned diagnostics the count multipliers. Method comparisons that include REML or residual contrasts retain each complete single-method object in method_results, so distinct bases and centers are not conflated by the combined table. For MLS SEM, individual-plan tables additionally retain ErrorVariance, ErrorVarianceSE, RawVarianceLower and RawVarianceUpper in squared score units. The squared ErrorVarianceSE uses the unbiased df + 2 sampling-variance formula described in confint.mfrm_multivariate_gstudy(); no delta-method SEM SE is supplied. diagnostics retains component and mean-square weights indexed by plan, and mean_squares retains the scale and source df. With reference, rows exclude the reference plan, Metric is the selected metric followed by " difference", and Estimate is comparison minus reference. Reference, ReferenceCount, ReferenceValue, and Value retain the two plans' context. Attribute reference also retains its point status. For MLS SEM differences, it retains the reference SEM interval, raw error-variance bounds, estimate and SE in place of per-plan variance columns. Nested results also retain nesting_context with facet identities, the source children per parent, and both counts for every future plan. A nested reduction/MLS reference includes count_facet and children_per_parent. General region comparisons instead retain all reference counts, its interval, status and diagnostics; individual_intervals stores the planwise projections before forming the difference enclosure. Their diagnostics list aligns with comparison rows. No scalar ReferenceCount is invented for a comparison changing both facets. No sampling SE or covariance matrix is inferred from the interval width. Stored G-study summaries are used and point projections are recomputed without refitting for the summary-based methods; REML profiles fit the stored used ratings. Every method leaves the input unchanged.

Details

For a source-by-target choice table, see Choose the G-theory target and uncertainty in mfrmr_methods_reference. Incomplete-source calculations are available through explicit methods; this does not qualify a generally calibrated automatic default. Read the selected method's assumptions below.

Each interval concerns a population coefficient or SEM of a future plan: uncertainty comes from the source G-study, not from collecting the proposed future ratings. GENOVA-adjusted D-studies can use the same population-parameter intervals. Estimate and PointStatus describe the adjusted point; IntervalEstimate and IntervalPointStatus retain the original source-study projection. ComponentTreatment and IntervalBasis distinguish their bases. The original source mean squares, data, bounds, diagnostics and unavailable states are preserved; adjusted components never replace the source inputs. The bounds are not recentered and need not contain the adjusted point. An existing method-specific IntervalCenter remains separate from both. Where a method supplies a coefficient sampling SE, it is named IntervalSE for adjusted results. SamplingVariance, error-variance columns and other diagnostics also retain their original method basis. None describes the sampling distribution of the zero-substituted or EMS-recalculated estimator. In the method descriptions below, references to the original Estimate mean IntervalEstimate when component treatment is adjusted.

This distinction follows from the common population target: changing a reported point does not change the confidence-set event based on the source study. Exact procedures keep their stated normal-model qualifications; approximate or experimental methods do not become exact through adjustment. GENOVA's unchanged component SEs cannot be interpreted as an adjusted estimator's SE. Its truncation is nonsmooth at zero; an adjusted-estimator delta interval would require additional derivation and boundary validation. Saved intervals must match the D-study's treatment as well as its source. Use confint(d, reference = ...) for supported population plan differences; the separate mfrm_multivariate_d_compare() delta-estimator API still requires raw components.

For a balanced two-crossed-facet source, start with confint(d, parm = "Phi", assumption = "normal") for absolute dependability, or parm = "G" for relative ordering. Read Estimate, Lower, Upper, Status and FormulaComplete. The default is an approximation: a returned interval is not evidence that the model assumptions hold. Use plot(d, metric = "Phi", intervals = TRUE, assumption = "normal") to add its ribbon, and attr(ci, "notes") to read cautions saved with a result ci.

Two-crossed-facet MLS intervals

Under the balanced independent normal-effects model, mean squares M[j] are independent lambda[j] * chi-square(df[j])/df[j]. Let theta=A*lambda be the variance components, U=theta[Person], and E=error' theta the relative or absolute error variance for the prespecified future counts. A candidate rho=U/(U+E) is equivalent to the linear null h(rho)'lambda=0, with h(rho)'=((1-rho)e_P' - rho*error')*A. The denominator must be positive; positive source mean-square expectations and residual variance are assumed. No estimated ratio or component is clipped.

Compute the unrestricted Ting MLS interval for this signed linear combination and retain rho when it contains zero. The asymmetric chi-square/F corrections use source degrees of freedom. This is mfrmr's inversion of the published linear-combination construction; Ting et al. and Hess/Iyer do not directly establish coverage for this G/Phi procedure. The inversion inherits approximate, rather than exact, calibration. The checked two-term cases at the usual 95% level reproduce F inversion. This is not an identity for arbitrarily low confidence levels: squaring a reversed chi-square correction can lose its direction. The sampling evaluations below concern 95% intervals.

Between coefficient sign changes, the squared widths and squared null point are quadratic in rho. All polynomial crossings in [0,1] are evaluated, including sign-change points, where the MLS formula can be discontinuous. Diagnostics retain accepted pieces and individual nodes; Lower/Upper enclose their union. This avoids a finite grid or repeated model fitting. The polynomials use shifted and scaled coordinates to resolve narrow sets near a boundary. If root separation cannot be represented on the coefficient scale, bounds are missing with an explicit Status and NumericalComplete=FALSE; the point estimate is retained. This is distinct from a genuine empty set or a formula-defined endpoint at zero or one.

A squared MLS width can be negative for some candidate values, especially with few degrees of freedom and highly unequal components. Such candidates are conservatively retained rather than assigned a zero width or silently dropped. FormulaComplete=FALSE identifies this completion, and each row's attr(ci, "diagnostics") entry retains the undefined ranges. This can only enlarge the retained set; it cannot make the approximate calibration exact. A numerical inversion failure remains unavailable and is distinct from this defined completion rule. An empty set also remains explicit. An unavailable original ANOVA point does not prevent calculation of an interval.

Normal-model checks illustrate both potential and limits. In a matched 400-source study with 60 persons, 4 raters, 12 tasks and component variances (1,.2,.3,.3,.4,.1,1), the source-plan G interval had mean width .0945 and coverage .950; Phi had mean width .3287 and coverage .970. The conservative mean-square region gave widths .1974/.7249 and coverage 1/1 in those same samples. The component order is Person, Rater, Task, Person:Rater, Person:Task, Rater:Task, residual. A further eight-condition normal study used 2,000 sources per condition, Person counts 5–80, source facet counts from 2-by-2 to 2-by-20, zero/near-zero Person variance, dominant facets/interactions and changed future counts. All-attempt inclusion was .9505–.9885 for G and .948–1 for Phi after the stated completion. At .95, Monte Carlo SE is about .0049 with 2,000 sources. Some small-source Phi conditions returned [0,1] in over 90% of available cases. These are limited normal-model evaluations, not uniform coverage, robustness, or a promise of useful precision in every design. Increasing future counts does not compensate for a weak source design.

This choice supplies pointwise individual-plan intervals for balanced two- crossed-facet sources and prespecified scores/composites. It does not supply simultaneous curve bands, plan-difference intervals, or incomplete/nested- source inference. The exact one-facet G and generalized one-facet Phi defaults retain their different constructions. The name "mls" for SEM instead refers to a direct error-variance interval followed by a square root.

Interpreting the target and other defaults

More future tasks can improve G but do not increase the source degrees of freedom. A narrow interval is not guaranteed by a large proposed task count. G concerns relative ordering; these intervals do not give pass/fail accuracy, or Person-rank intervals. Phi includes the random measurement facet's main effect in absolute error; use it when absolute score levels matter.

The F pivot is exact under the balanced independent normal-effects model, with positive residual variance. It is not a distribution-robust interval for arbitrary numeric ordinal scores. It applies to a selected original score or a fixed linear composite, including prespecified difference scores. General two-facet plans and incomplete-source MINQUE(0) do not have this pivot. The nested unchanged-child-count subcase below does reduce to it. Balanced F/GCI, MLS, score and mean-square-region methods use stored ANOVA summaries. The score method fits null nuisance expectations to those summaries. One-facet Phi GCI draws independent chi-square quantities; it is not an exact frequentist-coverage guarantee. Spectral F and residual contrasts require retained ratings; delta uses ANOVA summaries or retained MINQUE assignments and moment inputs. REML profiles require used ratings and refit a separate model. These input requirements also apply to saved G-study objects; reopening already computed intervals does not refit them.

Score intervals for two-crossed-facet G

Explicit method = "score" uses the independent normal-theory mean-square sampling law of a balanced Person-by-two-random-facet source. For proposed G = \(\rho\), write the population target as \(\theta_P/(\theta_P+e^T\theta)\) and test \(h(\rho)^T\lambda=0\), where \(\theta=A\lambda\), \(h(\rho)^T=((1-\rho)e_P^T-\rho e^T)A\), and \(\lambda\) contains the positive mean-square expectations. Nuisance components may be negative as long as this restricted marginal covariance remains positive definite. These computational values do not replace the ANOVA components. The nuisance score is checked independently of optimizer status labels. If \(S_\lambda=\kappa h\), the expected-information statistic is \(T=\kappa^2\sum_j 2h_j^2\lambda_j^2/df_j\). Invert its approximate chi-square(1) test over \(0\leq\rho\leq1\).

This construction is motivated by Shedden and Ekvall's extended-nuisance score approach; their preprint does not establish G/Phi ratio intervals. For the active independent strata, the spectral/Frobenius bound in their asymptotic condition is \(1/\sqrt{\min_j df_j}\). G uses Person-containing strata, whose degrees of freedom increase with source Persons even with fixed facet counts. This does not give exact finite-sample coverage. A retained normal-model evaluation used 360 independent sources per condition, six conditions and three future plans: true-value inclusion was 93.1–97.8%, with Monte Carlo SEs of 0.8–1.3 percentage points. These checks test the statistic at the truth, not complete endpoint coverage. The lowest cell's exact binomial 95% interval was 89.9–95.5%. The method remains experimental and is never selected automatically.

The numerical inversion compares two finite grids, includes contrast sign-change locations, and verifies cutoff crossings. Diagnostics retain all scanned fits and accepted pieces; bounds are their envelope. These checks do not prove global nuisance optima or exclude narrower undetected pieces. NumericalComplete describes the completed numerical check. Empty = TRUE means the scanned confidence set is empty: it is not an estimate of zero or zero uncertainty. Empty sets and numerical failures both have missing Lower/Upper, but distinct status and diagnostics. CandidateLower/CandidateUpper retain exploratory bounds after failure. Cutoff-crossing errors must be smaller than min(1e-5, 1e-5 * critical). If this tolerance falls below 64 * .Machine$double.eps * max(1, critical), the cutoff is numerically unresolved: bounds are missing, NumericalComplete = FALSE and Empty = FALSE. Original points remain available; this is not an empty confidence set or a minimum sample-size restriction. Diagnostics retain critical, cutoff_tolerance, numeric_resolution, root_tolerance and grid_tolerance. Root and grid-comparison tolerances tighten for small critical values. These arithmetic checks do not certify global nuisance roots or complete confidence-set topology. Positive observed mean squares are required. Few source Persons can yield broad intervals or inaccurate calibration. The method is pointwise for a prespecified score/composite and future plan, with no distribution-robust or simultaneous-coverage claim.

Phi also depends on few-df facet strata. Extending this same score rule to Phi produced very broad sets and changes between nuisance roots near zero; it is therefore not offered for Phi. Separate score intervals cannot be subtracted to obtain a paired-plan difference interval.

REML profiles for balanced or incomplete sources

For a fixed score or composite, this method fits the normal random-effects model of the declared grouping assignment: one common mean and independent Person, facet, interaction and residual effects. Source omissions must be noninformative conditional on that fixed assignment. It does not model outcome-dependent missingness, unequal future exposure or selection of score weights from the observed data. The residual variance is positive. Raw used ratings are needed; ANOVA/MINQUE component summaries alone are insufficient for the incomplete-source likelihood.

Write the variance ratios as v, with residual ratio one. For each plan, let c contain its relative or absolute error divisors, with c[Person] = 0. The coefficient is rho = v[Person] / (v[Person] + sum(c * v)). Fixing a proposed rho eliminates the Person ratio as rho / (1 - rho) * sum(c * v). The remaining nonnegative ratios are optimized; the common mean and residual scale are profiled analytically using the restricted Gaussian likelihood. The accepted numerical set has deviance increase no larger than qchisq(level, df = 1).

For SEM, constrain the error variance tau = sum(c * theta) directly, where theta = s2 * v includes the positive residual variance s2. The profiled residual scale at fixed ratios is s2_hat(v). Restore it to the criterion using D(v,s2) = D_profile(v) + (n-1)*(log(s2/s2_hat) + s2_hat/s2 - 1). At fixed positive tau, substitute s2 = tau / sum(c*v) and optimize the remaining ratios. Take square roots of the error-variance endpoints and restore the original score units. This is a constrained likelihood for the error variance, not addition of component bounds or a delta method. The residual scale cannot be profiled freely while fixing an absolute variance target. SEM intervals describe sampling uncertainty in the population measurement SEM, not intervals for individual Person scores.

This is an implementation of target-specific restricted-likelihood inversion, not a MINQUE likelihood or a published exact G-theory pivot. Bates et al. describe the REML criterion and sparse computation, not a validation of these G/Phi or SEM intervals. It also differs from lme4's ordinary parameter-profile intervals, which use an ML criterion. The chi-square cutoff is asymptotic; a generic boundary mixture is not substituted. The special-case results of Crainiceanu and Ruppert illustrate why boundary calibration cannot be assumed for arbitrary multi-component designs.

A limited normal-model feasibility check used 40 samples per assignment and population condition. True-value likelihood-ratio acceptance ranged from 92.5% to 100% with positive components and from 87.5% to 100% in the checked zero-component populations, counting numerical failures as misses. These imprecise checks do not establish 95% coverage or general robustness, and true-value acceptance is not a full endpoint-performance study. Numerical endpoint calculations were separately checked on selected data. Use this explicit experimental option only with its qualifications; agreement with another interval in one dataset does not establish coverage.

A separate SEM feasibility check reused 40 samples per assignment and population. Positive-component true-value acceptance ranged from 92.5% to 100%; checked boundary populations ranged from 82.5% to 100%. The lowest result was absolute SEM in an incomplete crossed source with 30 persons, 4 raters and 5 tasks and zero facet/interaction variances; numerical availability there was 97.5% and the inclusion Monte Carlo SE was 6.0 percentage points. These are coarse warning signals, not evidence that nominal 95% inference is reliable. They concern acceptance at the true target, not coverage of all returned interval endpoints.

Three starting points, an independent BOBYQA optimization, and finite differences with boundary checks verify numerical solutions. For G/Phi, a grid including the REML estimate locates cutoff crossings; root finding refines them. Disconnected accepted pieces are retained in diagnostics, while Lower/Upper give their envelope. If the REML coefficient center rounds to one, the current coefficient-scale search is unavailable: bounds remain missing with an explicit numeric-resolution Status. The source optimization may still have passed its checks; the rounded center does not establish perfect reliability or zero uncertainty, and the uncomputed interval need not have zero width. This interval search also does not certify a global optimum or exclude narrow pieces missed between grid points. An unresolved profile or upper tail is flagged, with exploratory CandidateLower/Upper retained separately; it is not replaced by a zero-width or [0,1] interval. For a very small requested confidence level, a likelihood-ratio cutoff indistinguishable from numerical error leaves the interval unavailable. Endpoint tolerance is min(1e-5, 1e-5 * cutoff) and must exceed the floating-point resolution check 64 * .Machine$double.eps * max(1, abs(source_deviance)). Row-aligned diagnostics[[i]]$cutoff retains these values. This check does not certify optimizer accuracy. A positive interval width or nonzero endpoint lost on restoring score units also gives missing bounds with an explicit Status, keeping the original point and representable REML center. These checks apply to component, covariance, G/Phi, SEM and direct-difference profiles; an identical-plan direct contrast remains an exact zero when its source checks pass. Separate score and weight scaling preserves a composite under reciprocal changes of units.

For SEM, log1p variance-ratio coordinates retain exact zero components while reducing scale differences. Search outward from the REML center until the first checked cutoff crossing in each direction, then refine the roots and check their likelihood-ratio residuals. This returns a numerical interval around the center; it does not enumerate disconnected remote accepted regions. A finite scan cannot prove global nuisance optima or rule out narrower undetected crossings. Unresolved required evaluations, roots or tails retain unavailable bounds and separate candidates; reaching a search limit does not justify an infinite endpoint. Proportional error-weight vectors reuse the same profile by scaling the error-variance targets. This is an exact transformation, without new fits.

Estimate and PointStatus always retain the source ANOVA/MINQUE result. IntervalCenter is the REML estimate of the same population coefficient or SEM. A source point can be unavailable or outside the profile interval; fitting nonnegative REML variances does not repair the original component matrices. Forests and D-study curves retain the original source points. Save the interval object to avoid fitting again when plotting or reopening it. Individual-plan intervals are pointwise. The shared-profile differences below have a separate common-base justification. The normal assumption and a successful optimizer do not imply accurate finite-sample calibration.

Plan differences from one shared REML interval

With method = "reml_profile" and reference, compare one-facet plans or nested plans with the same future child count per parent. The child count may differ from the source. The observed assignment, including incomplete cells and unequal child counts, stays in the full REML model; it is not averaged or replaced by balanced data.

These future plans have error variance e0 / m, where m counts the measurement-facet levels or nested parents. For G/Phi, let t = U / e0, where U is Person variance. The coefficient at count m is m*t / (1+m*t). Calculate one base profile at count one, then map its whole interval through the comparison-minus-reference function. With counts b and a, its stationary point is t = 1/sqrt(a*b); this must be included when inside the base interval. Subtracting marginal confidence endpoints or transforming only the two base endpoints is wrong. For SEM, multiply the shared base interval for sqrt(e0) by 1/sqrt(b) - 1/sqrt(a), reversing limits when this factor is negative.

Whenever the base interval contains its population target, all returned images contain their true differences for this fixed score/composite. This event transfers the base method's coverage; it does not establish exact nominal coverage or remove numerical-search limitations. Mapping an envelope can be conservative, and SEM still uses the interval around its REML center. No additional model is fitted for each comparison. Original ANOVA/MINQUE differences remain in Estimate, with the REML differences in IntervalCenter. An unavailable base remains unavailable, even for identical plans; candidate images are exploratory only.

attr(result, "base_interval") retains the complete count-one interval and its profile diagnostics. Plot the comparison with plot(result); difference intervals cannot be used as individual-plan curve ribbons.

Direct REML profiles for other plan differences

For crossed plans or nested plans with different future child counts, the same call uses a direct difference constraint on the shared source likelihood. It does not subtract marginal confidence endpoints. Let a and b be reference and comparison error weights, v the variance ratios with residual ratio one, ea = sum(a*v), eb = sum(b*v) and U = v[1]. The G/Phi difference is U*(ea-eb)/((U+ea)*(U+eb)). A nonzero target can have two positive solutions for U, on either side of sqrt(ea*eb); both seed the search. At zero difference, fit both the zero-Person and equal-error branches. The equal-error solution also seeds nearby targets to avoid following only the zero-Person branch. Multiple starts and independent constraint and stationarity checks still cannot certify global optima.

The SEM difference is sqrt(s2)*(sqrt(eb)-sqrt(ea)), in standardized score units. The constraint therefore restores the residual scale in the full REML criterion. At zero SEM difference the errors must be equal; zero Person variance alone does not satisfy this null. Final SEM bounds are multiplied by the source score scale, retaining signed score units.

A grid and checked cutoff crossings retain detected accepted pieces; Lower/Upper enclose those pieces, not a guaranteed enumeration of the global set. attr(result, "diagnostics") retains each comparison's sets, scan, profiles, roots, numerical failures and candidate bounds. SEM diagnostic targets and sets are standardized; multiply by attr(result, "reml_source")$score_scale for the original score units. Required failed evaluations or unresolved tails leave accepted bounds unavailable. A search limit is not an infinite confidence bound.

These comparisons are pointwise and experimental, not simultaneous. Their chi-square(1) calibration and finite-sample coverage are not established generally. In particular, the two branches of the zero coefficient null intersect at a singularity. Drton (2009) explains why singularities and boundaries can invalidate ordinary likelihood-ratio calibration; that paper is not a derivation of the present G-theory method. Neither numerical completion nor a warning supplies a coverage guarantee. Prefer a method with justified coverage for the design and inferential purpose; use this explicit choice to examine the fitted likelihood while retaining its qualifications. It is never selected automatically.

Sampling uncertainty in measurement SEM

SEM describes measurement error in score units; its confidence interval describes how uncertain that population SEM is given the source study. It is not a confidence interval for a Person's score, a sampling SE of G, or an interval obtained by adding component confidence bounds.

Write the raw component estimates as A %*% MS. If w contains the future-count divisors for relative or absolute error, the error-variance estimate is w' A MS. Apply the normal-model interval to this one linear combination of independent mean squares, intersect it with nonnegative variances, then take square roots. This monotone transformation preserves the original interval's coverage event. It does not improve an approximate MLS interval's coverage. Component formulas and nested child-count units are given in mfrm_d_study(). With method = "mean_square_region", project the common simultaneous mean-square region onto each error variance, then take square roots. This retains conservative normal-model coverage, including joint coverage over future plans for the fixed score. It can be much wider than MLS and has no MLS sampling-SE columns; diagnostics retains variance-scale bounds.

The single-mean-square interval is exact under the stated normal model when its expectation is positive. For example, one-facet relative error is MS_residual / future_count. A nested relative error also reduces to one mean square when the future number of children per parent equals that in the source. Otherwise positive combinations use Graybill-Wang and signed combinations use Ting MLS, as set out by Hess and Iyer (2002). Betebenner (1998) applies these constructions to G-theory error variances. Both are approximations, not distribution-robust or simultaneous intervals. Their squared chi-square corrections can lose their usual direction at very low confidence levels; the sampling evaluation below concerns 95% limits. If a positive variance interval or its square-root image loses its width through numerical rounding, the SEM limits are missing and Status explains the loss of resolution. The original SEM and any calculable error-variance SE are retained. This also applies to residual-contrast SEM. An unavailable common source interval does not become a zero-width plan-difference interval, even for identical counts. Recompute confint(d, ...) from a saved D-study to apply current numerical checks; a G-study refit is not required.

A bounded check used nine normal-model source conditions with 2,000 replications each: one-facet, crossed and nested small/larger designs, including zero components. Each had three future plans and both SEMs. Across the 51 positive-error targets, nominal 95% coverage ranged from 93.45% to 99.00% (Monte Carlo SE 0.22–0.55 percentage points), and availability from 99.75% to 100%. The lowest coverage concerned absolute SEM with 10 persons, 2 raters and 3 tasks, projected to one rater and one task. The all-zero relative-error cases returned unavailable intervals. This limited check identifies undercoverage and conservatism; it is not a guarantee for other populations, designs or nonnormal scores.

For a one-facet source, every SEM is s / sqrt(m) for the same single-rating error SD s and future count m. With reference count a and comparison b, transform the whole interval for s by 1/sqrt(b) - 1/sqrt(a), reversing endpoints when negative. This retains dependence between plans. The common base coverage event protects all returned differences for that fixed score; relative SEM has exact normal-model coverage for positive residual variance, while absolute SEM retains approximate MLS coverage. Lower SEM differences favor the comparison plan. Identical counts give [0,0] only when the base interval is available. Nested comparisons with a common future child count use the same mapping in the parent count; their base may require Ting MLS. mfrm_multivariate_d_compare() retains its separate paired-delta scope.

Spectral F intervals for one-facet G

Use method = "spectral_f" when a one-facet source is incomplete or unequal and the independent normal-effects model is appropriate. The future plan must still be complete and balanced. Unlike residual-only SEM inference, this method requires normal Person effects as well as normal residuals. Assignment and omissions must preserve the assumed model.

Write the scalar or fixed-composite response as y = Z_P p + Z_F f + e, with Person variance sigma_P^2 and positive residual variance sigma_E^2. The facet incidence contains the intercept. Removing its column space also removes every realized facet effect without changing the population G target. Let U diag(sqrt(lambda)) V' be the thin singular decomposition of the projected Person incidence, keeping its r positive singular values. Then z = U' y has independent normal coordinates with variances sigma_E^2 + lambda_i * sigma_P^2. Projecting off both Person and facet incidence supplies independent S_E / sigma_E^2 ~ chi-square(nu), where nu = n - rank([Z_P, Z_F]).

For t = sigma_P^2 / sigma_E^2, F(t) = {sum(z_i^2 / (1 + lambda_i*t)) / r} / (S_E / nu) has an F distribution with r, nu degrees of freedom at the true ratio. This is a specialization of the spectral pivot family in E, Hannig and Iyer (2008), equations 3–7, using all positive Person eigenvalues in the numerator and pure residual directions in the denominator. It is not their fiducial procedure or Burch and Iyer's optimal choice among partitions. The pivot decreases with t. Invert its central probability interval on t >= 0; an empty intersection remains an empty set. Analytic brackets using the smallest and largest eigenvalues locate endpoints, followed by checked one-dimensional root finding on the log-ratio scale. There is no likelihood optimizer, arbitrary upper parameter limit or pivotal simulation.

Each future count m maps the same set by G_m = m*t/(1+m*t). With reference, map the entire set through the G difference, including any interior extremum; see Differences in G between plans. The common event protects all returned plans/differences for this prespecified score. G intervals have exact normal-model coverage; difference images may be conservative. This is not a joint guarantee across scores or metrics, or protection against nonnormality, residual dependence or selected weights.

In a balanced source all positive eigenvalues equal the source facet count, recovering the usual "exact_f" limits. In an incomplete source, removing facet directions can discard useful information. Exact coverage does not establish optimal precision: sparse, small sources can give very wide intervals. No remaining residual contrasts, unresolved projection rank/variation and failed roots are reported explicitly. The residual combines Person-by-facet interaction and observation error. Distinct log-ratio limits that round to the same G value are also marked unavailable on that numeric scale, rather than displayed as zero uncertainty. This also applies to nonconstant plan-difference images whose widths or nonzero endpoints are lost to rounding. Identical-count differences are exactly zero when their base set is available; they cannot bypass a failed base calculation. A genuine singleton {0} from intersecting the F set with nonnegative ratios retains Status = "Upper endpoint at zero"; it is distinct from coincident finite bounds caused by lost numerical resolution. Extremely small confidence levels can make the two F quantiles numerically indistinguishable. On the log-F scale, endpoint tolerance is the smaller of 1e-8 and 1e-5 times their separation. If it falls below 64 * .Machine$double.eps * max(1, abs(log_quantiles)), the interval is unavailable with an explicit reason. This is an arithmetic-resolution check, not a small-sample restriction or a test of the model assumptions.

Estimate retains the original ANOVA/MINQUE G or difference, including unavailable points; no replacement center or sampling SE is supplied. LogVarianceRatioLower/Upper concern log(Person variance/residual variance), where -Inf denotes zero. These differ from the mean-square-ratio fields of the balanced F method. The pivot attribute saves eigenvalues, normalized squared coordinates, residual mean square, df and root checks. endpoint_tolerance and quantile_resolution record the numerical checks. Source-matched summaries and ribbons can reuse saved results.

Residual-contrast SEM

For a one-facet source, relative measurement SEM at future count m is sigma_E / sqrt(m). Thus method = "residual_contrast" first obtains one residual variance interval using the projection in confint.mfrm_multivariate_gstudy(), then takes square roots and divides by sqrt(m). This applies to incomplete or unequal observed assignments that retain residual degrees of freedom. The future plan is still a complete balanced assignment; its counts do not describe the sparse source.

Under independent homoskedastic normal residuals and positive residual variance, the residual chi-square law is exact. Every plan interval is a monotone image of that same event. With reference, multiply the common residual-SD interval by 1/sqrt(comparison count)-1/sqrt(reference count); reverse endpoints for a negative multiplier. The common event protects all returned plans/differences jointly for this one prespecified score/composite. Identical-count differences are zero whenever the base interval is available. This does not provide a joint guarantee across different scores, metrics or adaptively chosen weights, nor robustness to selective omissions, nonnormal residuals or residual dependence. The source, not the future count, supplies the degrees of freedom and information.

Estimate and PointStatus retain the original ANOVA/MINQUE SEM or difference. IntervalCenter is the separately projected SEM or difference; both and the endpoints use score units. A negative original residual estimate can leave Estimate unavailable while the projected interval remains available. The original point is not replaced by the projected center or zero. No sampling SE of the original SEM estimator is supplied. The base_interval attribute retains the residual variance interval in squared score units, while residual_projection retains df and checks. No remaining contrasts, numerically unresolved variation or a failed base interval leaves limits unavailable, including for identical-count pairs.

Absolute SEM and multifacet SEM involve additional components; this transformation does not supply their intervals or G/Phi intervals. Use summary(d, intervals = TRUE, parm = "RelativeSEM", method = "residual_contrast", assumption = "normal") to collect supported results, or the same method in plot(d, type = "sem", metric = "RelativeSEM", intervals = TRUE, assumption = "normal") for curve ribbons. Save the complete result to reuse it without repeating the projection.

Nested plans

Suppose raters are nested within tasks: different raters serve each task, and every person is rated by all of them. If the source has three raters per task and every future plan also has three, task counts may vary while using confint() for G, Phi and their differences. This does not make the raters or tasks fixed. New random tasks and their random raters remain the generalization population.

Let R be the balanced source child count per parent. Within-cell means over the children have effective components vP, vParent + vChild/R, and vP:Parent + vResidual/R. Their mean squares are (MS_P, MS_Parent, MS_P:Parent)/R, with df (n-1, k-1, (n-1)*(k-1)), where k is the source parent count. They have the same independent normal-model sampling law as a one-facet G-study. Reuse the F/GCI calculations on this triplet and vary the parent count; no raw-data averaging or refitting is performed by confint(). For G, the residual-MS term in Wong and McGraw's (1999, p.277, equation 2.1.3) vanishes when the source/future child-count ratio is one. The GCI route is a reduction to the existing one-facet procedure, not a nested GCI attributed to that paper. G remains exact under the positive-error normal model; Phi retains approximate coverage and Monte Carlo diagnostics.

Changing the child count alters these effective components, so this coefficient reduction no longer applies. Individual SEM intervals still support changed child counts. For SEM differences, plans need only keep the same future child count as each other, which may differ from R: their common error SD scales by the inverse square root of the parent count. The base interval may then use signed-sum MLS, retaining its approximate coverage. Comparisons changing both nested counts are not supported by this default. Explicit method = "mean_square_region" comparisons permit both counts to change using the enclosure below. ReferenceCount in the reduction counts parents; general region comparisons instead retain all reference counts in attr(result, "reference")$counts. nesting_context retains children per parent and the original source design.

General nested coefficient calculations

Both counts can change with explicit "approximate_f" or "mean_square_region". Use the five components in order Person, parent, child(parent), Person:parent, residual. For future child/parent counts R,T, relative error weights are (0,0,0,1/T,1/(R*T)); absolute error adds (0,1/T,1/(R*T),0,0). The mean-square region has five independent mean squares rather than seven.

For the F calculation let n,r,t be source persons, children per parent and parents, and set m = r/R, h = t/T. The statistic is F(rho) = (1-rho)*MS_P/D(rho). For G, D = (1-rho+rho*h)*MS_P:parent + rho*h*(m-1)*MS_residual. For Phi, the coefficients of MS_parent, MS_child(parent), MS_P:parent, MS_residual are respectively rho*h/n, rho*h*(m-1)/n, 1-rho+rho*h*(1-1/n) and rho*h*(m-1)*(1-1/n). These follow by substituting the expected mean squares into the population coefficient, then isolating MS_P.

This agrees with Wong and McGraw's (1999, p.277) relative statistic. Their printed absolute formulas on p.278 omit the -rho*h/n term in the Person:parent coefficient and +rho*h/n in the residual coefficient. The implementation uses the expected-mean-square derivation above, checked against the component target and the unchanged-child one-facet reduction, rather than transcribing those printed formulas or their divided endpoints. No author-confirmed correction is claimed. Freeze the Satterthwaite df at the unrestricted ANOVA coefficient and invert the F inequalities, as for the crossed case. Signed denominator terms, negative components and invalid moments remain substantive limitations, not reasons to clip estimates.

A bounded normal-model evaluation reused 2,000 mean-square samples for each of three nested sources: 10 persons/2 children/3 parents, 60/4/8, and a 10/2/3 boundary model with only residual variance. Each had three future plans, with decreased, unchanged and increased child/parent counts. In the first two sources, nominal 95% approximate-F coverage was 93.55–96.45%, with 98.9–100% availability. In the boundary source projected to 4 children and 6 parents, coverage and availability both fell to 62.85% for G and 61.95% for Phi. Coverage retains unavailable replications in its denominator. A separate 200-sample region check gave 99.5–100% availability; some median coefficient widths exceeded .99. These limited results do not qualify either method as a generally useful automatic default.

Mean-square region calculation

For J independent normal-model ANOVA strata, each df[j]*MS[j]/lambda[j] has a chi-square distribution. Use marginal confidence level level^(1/J) for every expected mean square lambda[j]. Independence makes the joint rectangular region's coverage level. Intersect it with lambda = L * theta, where L is the expected-mean-square map and the scalar variance components theta are nonnegative. This retains the true component vector whenever the original region does.

Minimize and maximize theta[Person]/(theta[Person] + error' theta) over that common region for G/Phi. Positive residual limits and positive future counts keep this denominator positive. The change of variables z = theta/denominator, t = 1/denominator converts each endpoint problem to a linear program. SEM instead uses the extrema of the linear error variance, followed by square roots. The component scaling used internally changes coordinates, not the feasible set or target.

These projections can only increase coverage relative to the joint event for one prespecified score/composite. This does not guarantee narrow intervals. Empty intersections count as noncoverage in repeated sampling; coverage among only the returned intervals is a different quantity. The theoretical statement presumes correct projections; solver failures and finite-precision limitations remain separate availability conditions.

Extremely small confidence levels can make F quantiles or chi-square region limits numerically indistinguishable. The approximate-F calculation requires separation of log-F quantiles greater than 64 * .Machine$double.eps * max(1, abs(log_quantiles)). A region requires positive bounds with relative width (upper-lower)/upper greater than 64 * .Machine$double.eps for each expected mean square before optimization. Missing limits and Status explain failures; diagnostics retains F quantiles and resolution, or normalized mean_square_bounds, relative_width, region_resolution and the per-stratum tail probability. A SEM transformation that loses a nonzero endpoint or positive width is also unavailable. These checks retain the original point estimates and do not impose a minimum observation count.

Differences from a shared mean-square region

With reference and method = "mean_square_region", project the same simultaneous source region onto the reference and comparison targets. If their intervals are [L_a,U_a] and [L_b,U_b], report the enclosure [L_b-U_a,U_b-L_a]. The coverage justification is their common joint event, not independence or marginal 95% coverage. This is generally wider than the tight image of the difference over the region; it is not labeled exact.

Intersect with any sign restriction implied by componentwise ordering of the error weights. For example, if every error weight decreases, G/Phi cannot decrease and SEM cannot increase. For G/Phi, additionally intersect with the analytic population range. For positive reference/comparison errors ea, eb, the signed extremum of U*(ea-eb)/((U+ea)*(U+eb)) occurs at U=sqrt(ea*eb) and equals tanh(log(ea/eb)/4). Across nonnegative components, ea/eb lies between the smallest and largest active error-weight ratios a[j]/b[j]. Transform those limits and include zero to obtain FeasibleLower/Upper. These are parameter-space limits, not extra source information. Their intersection preserves the common-region coverage argument, including when an extremum is approached only as a limit.

Equal error weights give [0,0] only when the region projections are available. Preserve missing intervals and diagnostics even for identical plans. The common region event gives coverage of at least level jointly over the returned comparisons for one fixed score/composite under positive mean-square expectations and independent normal effects. It gives no distribution-robust guarantee, simultaneous guarantee across selected scores, or tightness guarantee. The returned individual_intervals and reference retain the projections. Original ANOVA/MINQUE points remain unchanged, even if outside the population range implied by nonnegative components.

Point estimates and intervals at boundaries

PointStatus describes the reported point estimate; Status describes the interval calculation. A negative ANOVA estimate of Person variance can make the point coefficient unavailable while a confidence interval still exists. Inspect both statuses; do not remove such an interval merely because Estimate is NA. An empty confidence set and a numerical failure are different outcomes, and neither means zero uncertainty.

A wide interval is retained: it may reflect limited information about the sampled persons, raters or tasks, as well as a conservative method. More numerical draws cannot supply information missing from the rating design. Clipping negative variance estimates or rejecting simulation draws changes a statistical procedure and does not by itself establish valid coverage.

Choosing a two-facet method

The approximate-F, mean-square-region, score and REML alternatives remain explicit choices alongside the default MLS method. Their coverage theory, precision and finite-sample evidence differ; see the method-specific sections. Available describes whether endpoints were computed; Validation and NegativeComponent describe separate limitations. A narrower interval is not automatically better. Select methods before inspecting which is most favorable, and retain unavailable rows when comparing performance.

  • Wong and McGraw (1999, pp. 275–276) give approximate F intervals for a fully crossed Person-by-two-facet random design. Both G and Phi use estimated Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. The authors advise against applying the method when variance-component estimates are negative. method = "approximate_f" implements the crossed-design calculation and the independently derived nested version above. Calculable intervals with negative components are retained as an experimental extension beyond that advice, with the flag set. Small normal-model evaluations found limitations in coverage, interval width and availability, particularly at zero components and when future facet counts change. See the G-theory vignette for conditions and results.

  • method = "mean_square_region" projects a simultaneous chi-square confidence region for the seven crossed or five nested independent expected mean squares onto nonnegative variance components. It is a conservative comparison based on normal ANOVA distribution theory, not a method attributed to Wong and McGraw. It can return almost the whole [0,1] range. It requires lpSolve; zero mean squares, infeasibility and numerical failures remain explicit.

  • method = "reml_profile" instead profiles the G/Phi target in a normal restricted likelihood, with approximate chi-square calibration. It also accepts identifiable incomplete/unequal sources. See the REML section above for the separate center, diagnostics and boundary limitations.

Use plot(result) for a forest comparison and plot_data() for its notes.

  • For balanced crossed G, method = "score" uses the extended-nuisance score construction above. Its treatment of nuisance component boundaries differs from the nonnegative REML profile; neither method is uniformly superior in the available finite-sample checks. Phi is unsupported.

To show one method along a planning curve, use plot(d, metric = "Phi", intervals = result) with matching score/composite selection; see plot.mfrm_multivariate_d_study(). Agreement of methods on one dataset does not establish robustness or frequentist coverage. The G-theory vignette includes small evaluation results with their denominators and Monte Carlo uncertainty.

Delta coefficient SEs and intervals

Use method = "delta" to quantify uncertainty in the original G/Phi coefficient without fitting a different estimator. Let \(U\) be estimated universe variance and \(E=a^T\hat\theta\) the relative or absolute error variance for the selected plan, where \(\hat\theta\) contains the original component estimates. For \(\hat\rho=U/(U+E)\), the gradient is \(g=\{(1-\hat\rho)e_U-\hat\rho a\}/(U+E)\), where \(e_U\) selects the universe component. The estimated sampling variance is \(g^T\hat C g\), with \(\hat C\) from vcov.mfrm_multivariate_gstudy(). The full covariance matters: estimated universe and error variances are not independent. Algebra uses normalized component scales to preserve invariance to score units and nonzero multipliers of fixed composite weights.

Balanced scalar ANOVA uses A %*% diag(2*MS^2/(df+2)) %*% t(A) for \(\hat C\). This agrees with the random crossed derivation of Almehrizi (2021, equations 21–25). Nested and incomplete sources use the same differentiable ratio with their own design-specific component covariance. Those extensions follow the delta calculation; they were not evaluated in that paper. Its simulations assess SE accuracy, not Wald interval coverage. The covariance correction does not make a nonlinear coefficient SE unbiased. A normal-reference justification also requires growing information for the components that affect the target; more source Persons alone need not suffice. For example, with a fixed number of random raters and positive rater variance, increasing Persons does not consistently estimate the rater-population variance entering Phi. The rater mean-square degrees of freedom stay fixed. This limitation differs from the exact F result for one-facet G, which eliminates that nuisance component under its stated normal model.

SE is coefficient sampling uncertainty, not measurement SEM. Bounds are Estimate +/- qnorm((1 + level)/2) * SE. They are returned without clipping to [0,1], even when wide, and summaries, forests and ribbons retain them. OutsideParameterSpace and AtBoundary identify limitations of the normal approximation; they do not mean the population coefficient can exceed its parameter space. Small facet pools, weak information, boundaries and nonnormal effects can impair coverage. Increasing future plan counts does not increase the source study's information. Intervals are pointwise for prespecified plans and weights, not simultaneous or selection-adjusted.

The original point must be defined. A nonfinite or negative projected sampling variance retains its status and does not supply an SE or interval. Zero first-order variance retains SE = 0, but does not justify a degenerate normal-reference interval. Positive SEs are also retained when the requested interval width rounds to zero; the limits are then NA with a numeric-resolution status. An indefinite estimated component covariance is flagged; a finite positive projection still returns an explicit approximation. Nothing is repaired to obtain a preferred interval. For paired two-crossed- facet differences, mfrm_multivariate_d_compare() retains its separately documented plug-in covariance, rather than the corrected covariance used here.

A limited normal-model evaluation reuses 2,000 independent samples per source below, with a fixed outcome-independent omission pattern retaining about 8/11 of the cells. Person and residual variances are 1; all other component variances are 0.2. Future plans are complete balanced ratings at the source pool counts; nested child counts are per parent. Entries are percentages. Coverage uses all 2,000 attempts, counting unavailable intervals as not covering; return rates are shown separately.
